Floating-point error handling

Source: R/errstate.R
errstate.Rd

xsf, like scipy.special, reports conditions such as a pole or a loss of precision through error codes rather than R conditions. These functions choose what each code does, after scipy.special.geterr(), seterr() and errstate(): "ignore" it, "warn" with a warning of class zuspecial_warning and zuspecial_<code>, or "raise" an error of class zuspecial_error and zuspecial_<code>_error. Each code is signalled once per call, with the number of elements that raised it and the first one's index.

Usage

sc_geterr()

sc_seterr(
  all = NULL,
  singular = NULL,
  underflow = NULL,
  overflow = NULL,
  slow = NULL,
  loss = NULL,
  no_result = NULL,
  domain = NULL,
  arg = NULL,
  other = NULL,
  memory = NULL
)

sc_errstate(expr, ...)

Arguments

all

Action for every code, memory included, applied before the named ones.

singular, underflow, overflow, slow, loss, no_result, domain, arg, other, memory

Action for that code: "ignore", "warn" or "raise". NULL leaves it unchanged.

expr

An expression to evaluate under the temporary actions.

...

Actions passed to sc_seterr() for the duration of expr.

Value

sc_geterr() returns a named character vector with one action per code. sc_seterr() returns the previous state, invisibly. sc_errstate() returns the value of expr.

Details

The defaults are SciPy's: every code is ignored except memory, which raises. The state lives in the option zuspecial.errstate, so parallel workers start from the defaults. Set it with sc_seterr(); a value set directly is completed from the defaults, and refused if malformed.

See also

https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.special.seterr.html

Examples

sc_geterr()
#>  singular underflow  overflow      slow      loss no_result    domain       arg 
#>  "ignore"  "ignore"  "ignore"  "ignore"  "ignore"  "ignore"  "ignore"  "ignore" 
#>     other    memory 
#>  "ignore"   "raise" 
sc_errstate(sc_gamma(-1), singular = "warn")
#> Warning: sc_gamma: singular in 1 element, first at index 1.
#> [1] NaN
